title: Cascading and Adaptive KV Cache Eviction with Layer Preferences
one_line_claim: Layer-aware adaptive KV cache eviction using preference-based allocation maintains model performance with only 3.2% of the KV cache by dynamically adjusting allocation across layers based on spatial and temporal attention patterns.
method_summary: CAKE assesses layer-specific cache preferences by computing spatial attention dispersion (entropy H) and temporal attention shift (variance V) across transformer layers. It allocates cache budgets proportionally to preference scores via cascading memory management that progressively removes less important tokens while respecting global memory constraints. An attention-shift-tolerant eviction indicator retains tokens based on mean attention weight and variance rather than static scores.

key_findings.finding: CAKE maintains model performance with only 3.2% of the KV cache
key_findings.quote: CAKE maintains model performance with only 3.2% of the KV cache and consistently outperforms current baselines across various models and memory constraints, particularly in low-memory settings.

key_findings.finding: CAKE achieves over 10x speedup in decoding latency compared to full cache on 128K token contexts
key_findings.quote: CAKE achieves over 10x speedup in decoding latency compared to full caching on 128K token contexts with FlashAttention-2.

key_findings.finding: CAKE achieves 48.63% reduction in peak memory usage with 128K context length compared to full cache
key_findings.quote: When compared to the full cache implementation, CAKE achieves an impressive reduction in peak memory usage of approximately 48.63% with a 128K context length.

limitations: Focuses on uniform memory budget constraints; does not address heterogeneous hardware constraints.
Performance depends on accurate computation of attention patterns during prefilling, which may be expensive for very long contexts.

relation_to_herald.shared: Both CAKE and HERALD address KV cache compression as a mechanism for inference efficiency, recognizing that compression can degrade quality and seeking to manage this trade-off.
differs_on: CAKE focuses on layer-aware static allocation strategy during prefilling based on attention patterns; HERALD predicts catastrophic failures from per-token logit dynamics during decoding.
CAKE is a compression method that decides where to remove tokens; HERALD is a failure detector that predicts when compression fails dangerously (looping, non-termination).
CAKE optimizes cache allocation based on observed attention patterns; HERALD uses logit-based time-series features to forecast onset of hazards.
